paragraphs: Brothers, do not be afraid of men’s sin. Love a person even in his sin, for that is the likeness of God’s own love, and the highest love there is on earth. Love everything God has made, the whole of it and each grain of sand. Love every leaf and every ray of God’s light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will see the divine mystery in all things. Once you have seen it, you will understand it a little more each day. In the end you will love the whole world with a love that holds everything in it. Love the animals. God gave them the beginnings of thought and a joy that nothing disturbs. Do not disturb it. Do not torment them, do not rob them of their happiness, do not work against God’s purpose. Man, do not boast that you are above the animals. They are without sin, while you, for all your greatness, foul the earth by your very presence on it and leave the mark of your filth behind you. Alas, this is true of nearly every one of us! Love children most of all, for they too are sinless, like angels. They are here to soften and purify our hearts, and in some way to lead us. Woe to anyone who offends a child! It was Father Anfim who taught me to love children. That kind, quiet man would often spend on sweets and cakes for the children the farthings people gave us as we wandered. He could not walk past a child without being touched. That was the sort of man he was.

There are thoughts that leave a man at a loss, above all when he looks at the sin of others. He wonders whether he should use force or humble love. Always settle on humble love. If you settle on that once and for all, you can conquer the whole world. Loving humility is wonderfully strong. It is the strongest thing there is, and nothing else compares with it.

Every day, every hour, every minute, go around yourself and look at yourself, and make sure the picture you give is a decent one. Say you pass a little child. You pass him spiteful, with ugly words, with an angry heart. You may not even have noticed the child, but he has seen you, and your ugly, ignoble image may stay in his defenseless heart. You do not know it, but you may have planted an evil seed in him, and it may grow. And all because you were not careful in front of the child, because you had not trained yourself in a watchful, actively kind love. Brothers, love is a teacher, but one has to know how to get it. It is hard to get, it costs a great deal, and it is won slowly, by long labor. For we must love not only now and then, for a moment, but always. Anyone can love now and then. Even the wicked can.

My brother asked the birds to forgive him. That sounds senseless, but it is right, because everything is like an ocean. Everything flows and runs together, and a touch in one place sets something moving at the other end of the earth. It may be senseless to ask the birds for forgiveness. But the birds would be happier near you, a little happier at least, and so would children and every animal, if you were a nobler person than you are now. It is all like an ocean, I tell you. Then you would pray to the birds too. You would be consumed by a love that takes in everything, in a kind of transport, and you would ask them to forgive your sin as well. Treasure this ecstasy, however senseless it may look to men.

My friends, pray to God for gladness. Be glad like children, like the birds of heaven. And do not let men’s sin trouble you in your work. Do not fear that it will wear your work away and keep it from being finished. Do not say, “Sin is mighty, wickedness is mighty, our evil surroundings are mighty, and we are alone and helpless. Our evil surroundings are wearing us away and keeping our good work from being done.” Flee from that gloom, children! There is only one way to be saved. Take the blame on yourself and make yourself answerable for the sins of all men. That is the truth, you know, friends. As soon as you sincerely make yourself answerable for everything and for everyone, you will see at once that it really is so, and that you are to blame for every person and every thing. But if you push your own laziness and weakness onto others, you will end by sharing the pride of Satan and complaining against God.

About the pride of Satan, this is what I think. It is hard for us on earth to grasp it, and so it is easy to fall into error and share in it, even to imagine that we are doing something grand and fine. Many of the strongest feelings and impulses in our nature, in fact, we cannot grasp on earth. Do not let that trip you up, and do not think it can excuse you for anything. For the Eternal Judge asks of you what you can grasp, not what you cannot. You will know that yourself later, for then you will see all things as they are and will not argue with them. Here on earth we are, so to speak, wandering off course. If we did not have the precious image of Christ before us, we would be undone and altogether lost, like the human race before the flood. A great deal on earth is hidden from us. But to make up for that, we have been given a precious, mysterious sense of our living bond with the other world, the higher world of heaven. The roots of our thoughts and feelings are not here, but in other worlds. That is why philosophers say that we cannot take in the reality of things on earth.

God took seeds from other worlds and sowed them on this earth. His garden grew, and everything came up that could come up. But whatever grows is alive only through its sense of touching other, mysterious worlds. If that feeling grows weak in you, or is destroyed, the heavenly growth in you will die. Then you will be indifferent to life, and even come to hate it. That is what I think.
_(h) Can a Man judge his Fellow Creatures? Faith to the End_

Above all, remember that you cannot be anyone’s judge. For no one can judge a criminal until he recognizes that he is just such a criminal as the man standing in front of him, and that he may be more to blame than anyone for that very crime. When he understands that, he will be able to judge. That sounds absurd, but it is true. If I had been righteous myself, perhaps there would be no criminal standing before me. If you can take upon yourself the crime of the criminal your heart is judging, take it at once. Suffer for him yourself, and let him go without a word of blame. And even if the law makes you his judge, act in the same spirit as far as you can, for he will go away and condemn himself more bitterly than you have done. Suppose that after your kiss he goes away unmoved and mocking you. Do not let that trip you up. It shows only that his time has not yet come. It will come in its own time. And if it never comes, no matter. If not he, then another will take his place, and will understand and suffer, and will judge and condemn himself, and the truth will be fulfilled. Believe that. Believe it without doubt, for in that lies all the hope and faith of the saints.

Work without stopping. Suppose you remember at night, as you go to sleep, “I have not done what I should have done.” Get up at once and do it. Suppose the people around you are spiteful and callous and will not listen to you. Fall down before them and ask their forgiveness, for in truth you are to blame that they do not want to listen. And if you cannot speak to them in their bitterness, serve them in silence and humility, and never lose hope. If all men abandon you and even drive you out by force, then, when you are left alone, fall on the ground and kiss it. Water it with your tears, and it will bear fruit, even though no one saw or heard you in your solitude. Believe to the end, even if all men went astray and you were the only one left faithful. Make your offering even then, and praise God in your loneliness. And if two of you are gathered together, then there is a whole world, a world of living love. Embrace each other tenderly and praise God, because His truth has been fulfilled, if only in the two of you.

If you sin yourself, and grieve to the point of death over your sins, or over a sudden sin, then be glad for others. Be glad for the righteous man. Be glad that if you have sinned, he is righteous and has not sinned.

If the evil that men do stirs you to anger and crushing distress, even to a wish for revenge on the evil-doers, avoid that feeling above all others. Go at once and look for suffering for yourself, as if you yourself were guilty of that wrong. Take that suffering and bear it, and your heart will be comforted. You will understand that you too are guilty, because you could have been a light to the evil-doers, like the one sinless man, and you were not a light to them. If you had been a light, you would have lit the way for others too, and the evil-doer might have been saved from his sin by your light. And suppose your light was shining and you see that men were not saved by it. Hold firm, and do not doubt the power of the heavenly light. Believe that if they were not saved, they will be saved later. And if they are not saved later, their sons will be, for your light will not die even when you are dead. The righteous man departs, but his light stays. Men are always saved after the death of the one who saves them. Men reject their prophets and kill them, but they love their martyrs and honor the very people they have killed. You are working for the whole, you are acting for the future. Seek no reward, for your reward on this earth is great: the spiritual joy that is given only to the righteous man. Do not fear the great or the mighty, but be wise and always calm. Know the measure, know the times, and study that. When you are left alone, pray. Love to throw yourself on the ground and kiss it. Kiss the earth and love it with an unceasing, consuming love. Love all men, love everything. Seek that rapture and ecstasy. Water the earth with the tears of your joy, and love those tears. Do not be ashamed of that ecstasy. Prize it, for it is a gift of God, and a great one. It is not given to many, only to the chosen.
_(i) Of Hell and Hell Fire, a Mystic Reflection_

Fathers and teachers, I ask myself, “What is hell?” My answer is that it is the suffering of being unable to love. Once, in an existence without end, beyond measure in time and space, a spiritual creature was given a power when he came to earth. He could say, “I am and I love.” Once, only once, he was given a moment of active, _living_ love. For that, earthly life was given to him, and with it times and seasons. And that happy creature turned the priceless gift away. He did not value it or love it. He scorned it and stayed hard. Such a one, after leaving the earth, sees Abraham’s bosom and speaks with Abraham, as the parable of the rich man and Lazarus tells us. He sees heaven and can go up to the Lord. But that is exactly his torment: to go up to the Lord without ever having loved, to be brought near to those who have loved, when he despised their love. For he sees clearly, and says to himself, “Now I understand. Though I thirst to love now, my love will have nothing great in it, no sacrifice, because my earthly life is over. Abraham will not come, even with one drop of living water (that is the gift of earthly, active life) to cool the burning thirst for spiritual love that is in me now, though I despised it on earth. There is no more life for me, and there will be no more time! Though I would gladly give my life for others, it can never be, for the life that could be sacrificed for love has passed, and now a gulf is fixed between that life and this existence.”

People speak of hell fire in a material sense. I do not go into that mystery, and I avoid it. But I think that if there were fire in the material sense, they would be glad of it. I imagine that in bodily pain their far greater spiritual pain would be forgotten for a moment. Besides, that spiritual pain cannot be taken from them, because the suffering is not outside them but inside. And if it could be taken from them, I think it would be even bitterer for those unhappy creatures. Even if the righteous in Paradise forgave them, seeing their torments, and called them up to heaven in their boundless love, that would only multiply their torments. It would wake in them a still keener, flaming thirst for a love that answers, a love that is active and grateful, and that is now impossible. Yet in the timidity of my heart I imagine that the very recognition of this impossibility would in the end console them. By accepting the love of the righteous along with the impossibility of repaying it, by this submission and the work of this humility, they will reach at last a certain likeness of the active love they scorned in life, something like its outward form.... I am sorry, friends and brothers, that I cannot put this clearly. But woe to those who have killed themselves on earth, woe to the suicides! I believe no one can be more wretched than they. They tell us it is a sin to pray for them, and outwardly the Church, so to speak, disowns them. But in my secret heart I believe that we may pray even for them. Love can never be an offense to Christ. For such as these I have prayed inwardly all my life, I admit it, fathers and teachers, and even now I pray for them every day.

Oh, there are some who stay proud and fierce even in hell, though they know the absolute truth for certain and see it plainly. There are some terrible ones who have given themselves over completely to Satan and his proud spirit. For these, hell is voluntary and consumes them forever. They are tortured by their own choice. They have cursed themselves, cursing God and life. They live on their vengeful pride like a starving man in the desert who sucks the blood out of his own body. But they are never satisfied. They refuse forgiveness, and they curse God who calls them. They cannot look on the living God without hatred, and they cry out that the God of life should be destroyed, that God should destroy Himself and everything He has made. And they will burn in the fire of their own rage forever, and long for death and annihilation. But they will not reach death....

Here the manuscript of Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov ends. I repeat that it is incomplete and in pieces. The biographical details, for instance, cover only the earliest youth of Father Zossima. As for his teaching and opinions, what we find is a collection of sayings that were plainly spoken on very different occasions. What he said in his last few hours has not been set apart from the rest, but its general character can be seen from what we have in Alexey Fyodorovitch’s manuscript.

In the end the elder’s death came quite unexpectedly. The people gathered around him that last evening knew that his death was near. Still, it was hard to imagine it would come so suddenly. On the contrary, as I said before, his friends saw him that night apparently so cheerful and talkative that they were convinced his condition had changed for the better, at least for a time. Even five minutes before he died, they said afterwards in amazement, there was no way of foreseeing it. He seemed suddenly to feel a sharp pain in his chest. He went pale and pressed his hands to his heart. Everyone got up from their seats and hurried to him. But though he was in pain, he still looked at them with a smile. He slid slowly from his chair to his knees, then bowed his face to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as if in joyful ecstasy, praying and kissing the ground, he quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God.

News of his death spread at once through the hermitage and reached the monastery. His closest friends, and those whose office made it their duty, began to lay out the body according to the ancient ritual, and all the monks gathered in the church. Before dawn the news reached the town. By morning the whole town was talking about it, and crowds were pouring out of town toward the monastery. But this will be told in the next book. I will only add here that before a day was over, something happened that was so unexpected, so strange, so upsetting and bewildering in its effect on the monks and the townspeople, that even after all these years that day of general suspense is still vividly remembered in the town.
